title: RL for Autonomous Coding — Aakanksha Chowdhery, Reflection.ai
talk_summary: Aakanksha Chowdhery argues that inference-time compute (majority voting, self-revision) only reliably helps where outputs are automatically verifiable, and that RL on verifiable rewards (unit tests, compilers) is the next scaling frontier for coding agents. The talk is mostly a research/recruiting narrative with little operational detail on how to run agent systems.

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate multiple candidate solutions and select/agree among them only when an automated verifier (unit tests, compiler, execution feedback) can score each candidate; without a verifier, majority voting gives little gain.
takeaways.evidence_quote: inference time scaling would work in scenarios where I have automated verification
takeaways.numbers: pass@k on DeepSeek rises with number of samples on Bench-verified; no specific figures given

takeaways.what_they_do: Use compilers, unit tests, and execution feedback as the reward/verification signal instead of a neural reward model, which they say suffers from reward hacking.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you have execution feedback, you have unit tests. So all of these possibilities ... mean that you can design better reward functions

takeaways.what_they_do: Have the model sequentially revise its prior answer, evaluating against a checkable criterion, rather than accepting the first output.

takeaways.technique: Cheap inference-time scaling over expensive retraining
takeaways.what_they_do: Frames extra inference samples as cheap relative to training; spend inference compute where verification exists rather than upgrading model size.
takeaways.evidence_quote: inference calls are so cheap ... if you could get the models to generate multiple responses and then do majority voting
